summary.overview: Biomolecules are built from a small set of functional groups. Knowing how each group behaves (polar or not, acidic or basic, electrophilic, energy-rich) lets you predict what sugars, lipids, amino acids, nucleotides and coenzymes will do.

sections.heading: Hydrocarbons, alcohols, ethers and phenols
points: Aliphatic hydrocarbons (chains) and aromatic rings are non-polar: they form lipid tails and hydrophobic side chains.
Alcohols (R–OH) are polar H-bond donors and acceptors; sugars carry many hydroxyl groups.
Phenols have –OH on an aromatic ring and are more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised (e.g. the Tyr side chain).
Ethers (R–O–R′) are relatively unreactive; epoxides are strained three-membered rings and are very reactive.

sections.heading: Aldehydes and ketones
points: Both contain a carbonyl group (C=O). Aldehydes have it at the end of a chain (–CHO); ketones have it between two carbons.
The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (δ⁺), so nucleophiles such as alcohols add to it. This is how sugars form hemiacetal and hemiketal rings.
Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids or reduced to primary alcohols; ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.
Aldoses (e.g. glucose) carry an aldehyde group; ketoses (e.g. fructose) carry a ketone group.

sections.heading: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives
points: Carboxylic acids (–COOH) have pKa ≈ 2–5, so at physiological pH they exist as carboxylate anions (–COO⁻).
Esters form when an acid condenses with an alcohol (losing water); triacylglycerols are glycerol esters, hydrolysed by lipases.
Thioesters (e.g. acetyl-CoA) are less resonance-stabilised than oxygen esters, so they are excellent acyl-group donors.
Amides are the most stable derivatives; the peptide bond is an amide.
Acid anhydrides and acyl chlorides are very reactive. Phosphoanhydride bonds in ATP and the acyl phosphate of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate are biological high-energy anhydrides.

sections.heading: Nitrogen compounds and heterocycles
points: Amines (primary, secondary, tertiary) are basic and are protonated (–NH3⁺) at physiological pH. Proline contains a secondary amine.
Amides are not basic: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl, which also makes the peptide bond planar.
Nitriles (–C≡N): cyanogenic glycosides in some plants release HCN when the plant is damaged.
Heterocycles contain N, O or S in a ring: purines and pyrimidines (nucleic-acid bases), imidazole (His), indole (Trp), thiazole (thiamine), and pyranose and furanose rings (sugars).

keyTerms.definition: C=O, found in aldehydes, ketones, acids and their derivatives.
–COO⁻, the deprotonated form of a carboxylic acid at physiological pH.
R–CO–O–R′, formed from an acid and an alcohol.
R–CO–S–R′, an energy-rich acyl carrier, e.g. acetyl-CoA.
R–CO–NR′2; the peptide bond is an amide.
Bond between two phosphate groups, as in ATP.
Ring containing at least one atom other than carbon (N, O, S).

examTips: Amines are basic; amides are NOT, because the lone pair is delocalised.
At pH 7.4, carboxylic acids are carboxylates (–COO⁻) and amines are –NH3⁺.
Aldehyde → (oxidation) carboxylic acid; aldehyde → (reduction) primary alcohol.
Imidazole = His, indole = Trp; adenine and guanine are purines, while C, T and U are pyrimidines.

questions.stem: Glucose carries several –OH groups attached to sp³ carbons. What are these groups called?

options.text: Hydroxyl groups (alcohol groups)
options.why: R–OH on a saturated carbon is an alcohol; these make sugars very water-soluble.

options.text: Carboxyl groups (acid groups)
options.why: Carboxyl is –COOH, a carbonyl and a hydroxyl on the same carbon.

options.text: Ether groups (C–O–C links)
options.why: Ethers are C–O–C with no hydrogen on the oxygen.

options.text: Phenol groups (aromatic –OH)
options.why: Phenols have –OH on an aromatic ring, not on sp³ carbons.

questions.stem: The Tyr side-chain –OH (a phenol, pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than the Ser side-chain –OH (an alcohol, pKa ≈ 16). Why?

options.text: Resonance spreads the phenoxide's negative charge around the aromatic ring, stabilising it
options.why: A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid.

options.text: Serine's –OH is attached to an aromatic ring, which pulls electrons away from the O–H bond
options.why: Serine's –OH is on an aliphatic CH2; tyrosine's is on the ring.

options.text: Phenols contain a carbonyl group next to the –OH, which makes the proton easier to lose
options.why: Phenols have no C=O.

options.text: Alcohols are already negatively charged at pH 7, so serine's –OH cannot lose another proton
options.why: Alcohol –OH groups are essentially never ionised at physiological pH.

questions.stem: Why are epoxides much more reactive than ordinary ethers such as diethyl ether?

options.text: The three-membered C–C–O ring is highly strained, so nucleophiles open it readily
options.why: Releasing ring strain drives the reaction; reactive epoxides can damage DNA and proteins.

options.text: Epoxides contain a carbonyl carbon, which is attacked by nucleophiles just like an aldehyde
options.why: An epoxide has a C–O–C ring, not a C=O.

options.text: Epoxides are ionic compounds, so they dissociate in water into reactive charged fragments
options.why: They are covalent molecules.

options.text: Ordinary ethers have much weaker C–O bonds, so they break apart before they can react
options.why: Unstrained ether C–O bonds are relatively strong and stable.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?

options.text: In an aldehyde the carbonyl is at the chain end (–CHO); in a ketone it lies between two carbons
options.why: This is the difference between aldoses, such as glucose, and ketoses, such as fructose.

options.text: Aldehydes contain a nitrogen atom next to the carbonyl group, whereas ketones contain none
options.why: Both are C, H, O compounds.

options.text: Ketones carry an –OH group on the carbonyl carbon itself, whereas aldehydes carry a hydrogen
options.why: That would make a carboxylic acid.

options.text: Aldehydes have no C=O double bond; only ketones have a true carbonyl group
options.why: Both contain a carbonyl (C=O) group.

questions.stem: Glucose closes into a ring when its C-5 hydroxyl attacks the C-1 aldehyde. Why is the aldehyde carbon the target?

options.text: Oxygen pulls electrons from the carbonyl carbon, leaving it electrophilic, so –OH adds to form a hemiacetal
options.why: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls is one of the most common reactions in biochemistry.

options.text: The aldehyde carbon carries a full negative charge, so it attracts the slightly positive H of the C-5 –OH
options.why: It carries a partial positive charge, not a negative one.

options.text: The C=O bond is non-polar, so the C-5 hydroxyl can add across it without any repulsion from the oxygen
options.why: It is strongly polarised towards oxygen.

options.text: The aldehyde carbon is the most reduced carbon in glucose, so it is the easiest one to attack and oxidise
options.why: C-1 is the most oxidised carbon in glucose.

questions.stem: Acetaldehyde, formed in the liver from ethanol, is converted to acetate by aldehyde dehydrogenase. What type of reaction is this?

options.text: Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid
options.why: The –CHO becomes –COOH (acetate at physiological pH); NAD⁺ accepts the electrons.

options.text: Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol
options.why: Reduction would give back ethanol, a primary alcohol.

options.text: Hydrolysis of an ester into an acid and alcohol
options.why: Acetaldehyde is not an ester.

options.text: Condensation forming an amide with release of water
options.why: No amine is involved.

questions.stem: Lactic acid has a pKa of about 3.9. In which form is it mainly found in blood at pH 7.4?

options.text: As the lactate anion (–COO⁻)
options.why: When pH is far above the pKa, the carboxyl group is almost entirely deprotonated.

options.text: As undissociated lactic acid (–COOH)
options.why: That form predominates only when pH is below the pKa.

options.text: As a 50:50 mixture of the two
options.why: A 50:50 mixture occurs only at pH = pKa (≈ 3.9).

options.text: As a positively charged ion
options.why: Loss of H⁺ from a carboxyl group gives a negative ion.

questions.stem: Triacylglycerols, the main storage fats, contain which type of bond between glycerol and the fatty acids?

options.text: Ester bonds, formed between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol
options.why: Glycerol's three –OH groups are esterified; lipases hydrolyse these bonds.

options.text: Amide bonds, formed between a carboxylic acid and an amine
options.why: Amides need an amine; glycerol has none.

options.text: Phosphoanhydride bonds, formed between two phosphate groups
options.why: Those join phosphate groups, as in ATP.

options.text: Glycosidic bonds, formed between a sugar and another alcohol
options.why: Glycosidic bonds join sugars.

questions.stem: Acetyl groups are carried as the thioester acetyl-CoA rather than as an oxygen ester. Why is a thioester a better acyl donor?

options.text: The C–S bond is less resonance-stabilised than an oxygen ester, so acyl transfer releases more energy
options.why: The poorly stabilised ground state gives thioesters a high acyl-group transfer potential.

options.text: Sulphur is more electronegative than oxygen, so it pulls electrons away from the carbonyl carbon
options.why: Sulphur is less electronegative than oxygen.

options.text: Thioesters are far less reactive in water, so the acetyl group cannot be lost before it is used
options.why: Thioesters are reactive; that is why they are useful as donors.

options.text: A thioester contains a phosphoanhydride bond, which stores the energy needed to transfer the acetyl
options.why: Acetyl-CoA's energy-rich bond is the thioester itself.

questions.stem: The bonds linking the α, β and γ phosphate groups of ATP are which type of bond?

options.text: Phosphoanhydride bonds
options.why: Two phosphoric acid groups joined with loss of water form an anhydride, which releases a lot of energy on hydrolysis.

options.text: Phosphoester bonds
options.why: The bond joining the α-phosphate to ribose is a phosphoester; the bonds between phosphates are anhydrides.

options.text: Phosphodiester bonds
options.why: Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides in DNA and RNA (and close the ring of cAMP); ATP's phosphates are joined by anhydrides.

options.text: N-glycosidic bonds
options.why: The N-glycosidic bond links adenine to ribose, not the phosphate groups to each other.

questions.stem: Lysine's side-chain amine is protonated at pH 7, but the nitrogen of a peptide bond is not basic. Why?

options.text: In an amide the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl, so it can't accept a proton
options.why: Resonance also gives the peptide bond partial double-bond character, making it planar.

options.text: Amide nitrogens have no lone pair, because their outer electrons are used in bonds to carbon
options.why: The lone pair exists but is delocalised.

options.text: The peptide nitrogen is already permanently positively charged, so it cannot take another proton
options.why: It is neutral at physiological pH.

options.text: Amines are acids and amides are bases, so only the amine side chain gives up a proton at pH 7
options.why: Amines are bases; amides are essentially neutral.

questions.stem: Proline's amino nitrogen is bonded to two carbon atoms within a ring. How is this amine classified?

options.text: A secondary amine
options.why: N bonded to two C atoms (and one H) is secondary; it is often called an imino acid.

options.text: A primary amine
options.why: A primary amine's N is bonded to one carbon, as in the other standard amino acids.

options.text: A tertiary amine
options.why: A tertiary amine's N is bonded to three carbons; this happens only when proline forms a peptide bond.

options.text: A quaternary ammonium
options.why: A quaternary ammonium nitrogen carries four carbons and a permanent positive charge; proline's nitrogen has two carbons.

questions.stem: Cattle grazing wilted or frost-damaged sorghum can die suddenly. The plant contains cyanogenic glycosides, which carry a nitrile (–C≡N) group. What is released, and what does it inhibit?

options.text: Hydrogen cyanide (HCN), which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria
options.why: Damage to the plant releases HCN from the glycoside, which blocks the respiratory chain and causes acute cellular hypoxia.

options.text: Ammonia, which inhibits glycolysis and causes hepatic encephalopathy in the brain
options.why: The toxic product of the nitrile group is cyanide.

options.text: Nitrite, which forms carboxyhaemoglobin and so blocks oxygen transport in the blood
options.why: Nitrite forms methaemoglobin, and it comes from nitrate, not from cyanogenic glycosides.

options.text: Free glucose, which causes severe hyperglycaemia and inhibits insulin secretion
options.why: The sugar released is not the toxic part.

questions.stem: Which pairing of heterocycle and biomolecule is correct?

options.text: Imidazole: the histidine side chain
options.why: His's imidazole ring (pKa ≈ 6) makes it a key acid–base catalyst and buffer.

options.text: Pyrimidine: adenine (a DNA base)
options.why: Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines.

options.text: Indole: the histidine side chain
options.why: Indole is the side chain of tryptophan.

options.text: Thiazole: the tyrosine side chain
options.why: The thiazole ring is in thiamine (vitamin B1); tyrosine contains a phenol.

questions.stem: Pyruvate is CH3–CO–COO⁻. Which functional groups does it contain?

options.text: A ketone and a carboxylate
options.why: The middle carbon is a carbonyl between two carbons (ketone); the end carbon is a deprotonated carboxyl.

options.text: An aldehyde and an alcohol
options.why: There is no –CHO and no –OH.

options.text: An ester and a ketone
options.why: An ester would need C–O–C linking an acyl group to an alcohol part.

options.text: An amide and a carboxylate
options.why: Pyruvate contains no nitrogen.

flashcards.back: Alcohol: –OH on an sp³ carbon (pKa ≈ 16). Phenol: –OH on an aromatic ring, more acidic (pKa ≈ 10), e.g. Tyr.
Ether: R–O–R′, fairly unreactive. Epoxide: strained 3-membered C–C–O ring, very reactive.
Aldehyde: terminal –CHO (aldoses, e.g. glucose). Ketone: C=O between two carbons (ketoses, e.g. fructose).

flashcards.front: Typical reaction of a carbonyl carbon?
flashcards.back: Nucleophilic addition: it is electrophilic (δ⁺). Alcohol + aldehyde gives a hemiacetal (sugar ring formation).
Ester R–CO–O–R′ (fats). Thioester R–CO–S–R′ (acetyl-CoA, high transfer potential). Amide R–CO–NR′2 (peptide bond, most stable).
Phosphoanhydride bonds in ATP; the mixed acyl–phosphate anhydride in 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
Amines are basic (–NH3⁺ at pH 7). Amides are not basic: the lone pair is delocalised onto C=O.
Purines (two rings): adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines (one ring): cytosine, thymine, uracil.

flashcards.front: Which heterocycle is in His, Trp and thiamine?
flashcards.back: His: imidazole. Trp: indole. Thiamine: thiazole (plus a pyrimidine).
